questions.prompt: Something you owned end to end, including what went wrong.
beats: Hook: three occupied towers lose their fire alarm for a few hours · 16 nodes · ~1,500 devices · crew of 12 · I own it end to end
Built every panel on site a month early → 4 missing critical parts caught in time to ship
Fiber never jumpered, no redlines → light source, panel by panel, every run labeled
Defined roles · bar for going home set before we started: proven, not sampled
Result: under 8 hours impaired, fire watch throughout → ownership starts a month before the outage
End on what you changed afterward (the radios)
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: Walk me through the Cx levels for a pre-action system.
questions.followUp: Which level proves the water delivery time, and what do you record there?
beats: L1 factory acceptance: releasing panel factory test — equipment meets spec before it ships
L2 delivery and installation verification: what arrived matches the submittal and is installed per design and listing
L3 start-up / pre-functional: dry / pre-action air test; program loaded; 100% point-to-point
L4 FPT: pre-action trip with water delivery time, every sequence including failure and degraded modes, against the BOD
L5 IST: fire alarm through a utility failure onto generator; release signals to BMS / EPMS; NFPA 4 integrated test
End on IST: "At L4 I prove the system. At L5 I prove the building."
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

questions.prompt: A decision you made without complete information.
beats: Name the unknown: 8 COLOs · 20 VESDAs · no drawings — waiting wasn't an option
Pulled data first: all 20 at factory defaults
Counted holes, paced runs → only 4 pipe variations → 4 designs, not 20 (80% less)
Thresholds, airflow, transport time on every pipe; damaged pipe found and fixed
Cause and effect caught a wrong-COLO release → every inherited system is unverified
Why waiting was worse, and how you contained the risk
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: How do sprinklers work with hot-aisle containment?
questions.followUp: A field reroute adds fittings to get around the containment — what then?
beats: It is an obstruction question first
Containment panels listed to drop away on heat
or sprinklers inside the contained aisle
Hazard classification is set by the owner's and insurer's standard — FM Data Sheet 5-32 wants sprinklers throughout
A reroute that adds fittings changes the calc: recalc against the supply test, not a judgment call on the ladder
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

questions.followUp: You're a design engineer today — why move into commissioning?
beats: The loop: you build capacity in months and run what you build — 18 years in that loop on fire systems
Productizing the data center moves fire protection commissioning left: L1 scripts at the factory, the site tests interfaces
I build fire protection tools with frontier models; Fluidstack builds the infrastructure those models run on
Story 5 plus the research in the playbook
Follow-up: sell the bridge, not the switch — you design it, program it and commission it
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: Write the IST fire scenario for a data hall.
questions.followUp: What do you log if a panel throws troubles on transfer?
beats: Halls at full load-bank heat on normal power
ASD Fire 1, then Fire 2 or a second detector → pre-action valve trips
Inspector's test simulates a fused head
Verify notification, central station, valve trip and water delivery time, BMS / EPMS responses, cooling stays up
Drop utility mid-event → fire alarm on secondary power, pumps on generator, controllers transfer
Restore and verify every isolation reversed
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

questions.prompt: A time you rejected a standard approach.
beats: Texas BESS · 20 flame detectors · fault appears past ~7 connected
Measured, didn't hunt: 0.5–4 V induced per leg → ~7 modules sum past 0.4 V
Shielded, untwisted: a shield blocks electric fields, twisting cancels magnetic
Client tried cheaper fixes → I proved it with twisted cable laid on the ground
Re-pull ~2 weeks, commissioned → check cable data sheets at submittal
Show the reasoning chain, not the rebellion
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: The fire pump misses the 150% point at acceptance.
questions.followUp: The test setup checks out and it still misses — what then?
beats: Check the test first: calibrated gauges, pitot readings, nozzle sizes, measured speed with affinity correction
Then suction: a partly closed valve, strainer debris, air entrainment
Then the pump: rotation, impeller debris
Compare to the certified shop curve
Genuine shortfall = manufacturer claim and an impairment plan
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

questions.prompt: The schedule says skip or compress a test. What do you do?
questions.followUp: What did that cost the schedule, and who signed the risk acceptance?
beats: Sort it three ways
Life-safety and code-required tests are not negotiable
Tests that can run in parallel get re-sequenced
Anything deferred gets a documented risk acceptance, an impairment entry and a fire watch
"Velocity is knowing which unknowns actually block you" — their words, your method
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: Tell me about working with a third-party commissioning agent or an AHJ.
questions.followUp: What makes a test day go right?
beats: High-rise lab: ran the subs, programmed the fire alarm, contractor's liaison to the third-party Cx FPE — on the receiving end of every Cx script
Tested smoke control and the generator backup for the emergency circuits; main troubleshooter on fan and damper monitoring
Ran the AHJ inspection and trained the owners before turnover
A script they've seen in advance, a pre-test that has already passed, one person running the room
That's how I'd run it from the commissioning seat

questions.followUp: What would you do differently in the moment?
beats: Own your part first: 7 months in · SF data center · dirty head
No test mode, didn't pull the head, canned air from under the floor
Alarm → evacuation → fire department at rush hour
Didn't reset; confirmed, silenced, met the trucks and owned it
On test first · isolation-to-return-to-normal scripts · vacuum, don't blow → nobody learns about your test from an evacuation
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: A clean agent room fails its door fan test a week before turnover.
questions.followUp: Turnover is going ahead anyway — what do you document?
beats: Find leaks under depressurization (smoke pencil, thermal camera)
Cable and conduit penetrations, raised floor, ceiling plenum, dampers
Seal and retest
Never just add agent — that changes concentration against NOAEL and the overpressure vent sizing
If turnover proceeds, document the risk acceptance
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

questions.prompt: Tell me about a disagreement with a contractor or another trade during testing.
beats: Facts in the script
Criteria from the BOD
Escalate on the issues log
Never in the hallway

questions.prompt: Why not clean agent on a lithium-ion battery fire?
questions.followUp: So what does protect the rack?
beats: Agent does not cool cells in thermal runaway
Re-ignition follows once concentration decays
Water cools
Off-gas detection buys minutes
Vent gas is flammable, so explosion control matters

questions.prompt: What keeps you in this field — what do you do outside work?
questions.followUp: Which tool matters most for this role?
beats: "Turn what one expert knows into something the next person can repeat"
4 playbooks in company use → fewer go-backs, more techs can go
Thermal detection training with the manufacturer + my own camera placement tool
Night tools: EST3→EST4 priced BOM; panel capture that checks off the points list
"Productizing a data center is the same job"
